summary: This informational document specifies generic requirements for a protocol that lets Path Computation Clients ask Path Computation Elements for paths, and lets PCEs cooperate with each other. Later documents give application-specific requirements for the PCE communication protocol.

eli5.summary: If a trip planner exists, you need a standard way to ask it questions. This lists what that way of asking must be able to do.

what are pce communication protocol requirements
what constraints can a pce request include
subtitle: The checklist a protocol must satisfy so routers can ask a path computation server for routes.

tldr.problem: In the PCE model, a client asks a Path Computation Element (PCE) to compute a network path, but no protocol existed for that conversation, and the requirements for one were not written down.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists generic requirements for a PCE communication protocol (PCECP): request and response contents, constraints, objective functions, reliability, security, scalability, policy, liveness detection and recovery.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and generic only; application-specific requirements were left to later documents. It specifies no protocol itself.

today: RFC 4657 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements only; it defines no protocol and leaves application-specific requirements to separate documents.

sections.title: The PCE Model and Why It Needs a Protocol
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes network paths on request from a Path Computation Client (PCC). The PCC may be co-located with the PCE (composite) or remote from it (external). When they are not co-located, a request/response protocol is needed to carry the request and return the answer. The PCE works on a network graph built from the Traffic Engineering Database (TED), and how the TED is filled is out of scope.

A request includes at least the source and destination, and may add constraints and an objective function. A positive response carries the computed paths. A failed or impossible computation gets a negative response that indicates the type of failure. A single protocol is assumed for both PCC-PCE and PCE-PCE communication, and the requirements apply to all four PCE models in RFC 4655, though a composite PCE needs no protocol.
sections.eli5: A trip planner that gives directions to other machines needs a language for asking and answering. This RFC lists what that language needs to be able to say.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Messages
sections.content:
A request MUST include at least the source and destination, which are the start and end of the LSP or LSP segment to compute. It MUST support a set of constraints and let the requester choose from an advertised list of objective functions, with parameters, and vendor-specific or experimental ones. It MUST let the PCC state the metric type (IGP or TE) for shortest path selection, and whether load-balancing across several paths is allowed, with a maximum number of paths, a minimum path bandwidth and the required disjointness.

Responses MUST be able to return any explicit path usable as an Explicit Route Object in RSVP-TE signaling, made of strict or loose hops. They MUST allow path attributes such as cost and computed bandwidth. A negative response MUST be sent when no path is found, and MAY give reasons and advice on which constraints to relax.

Beyond that, a PCC MUST be able to cancel a pending request. Several requests MUST fit in one message, and responses can be spread over a sequence of correlated messages. The PCC MUST be able to state maximum response sizes. Communication MUST be asynchronous, so a PCC does not wait for one answer before sending another request, and responses MUST carry a direct correlation to their request. A PCC MUST be able to state the priority of a request, and unsolicited notifications in either direction MUST be supported.
sections.eli5: A question to the planner says where from, where to, and any rules like 'avoid this road'. The answer is a route or a clear 'no, and here is why'. You can ask many questions at once and take back a question you no longer need.

sections.title: Constraints and Objective Functions
sections.content:
The protocol MUST support at least these generic constraints: bandwidth, affinity inclusion or exclusion, link, node and Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) inclusion or exclusion, maximum end-to-end IGP metric, maximum hop count, maximum end-to-end TE metric, and degree of path disjointness (link, node, SRLG). MPLS-TE adds class-type, local protection, node protection and bandwidth protection. GMPLS adds switching type, encoding type and link protection type.

An objective function is the optimization criterion the PCE uses to pick the best candidate path. The protocol MUST support these unsynchronized functions: minimum cost path for a specified metric (shortest path), least loaded path, and maximum available bandwidth path. It MUST support these synchronized functions: minimize aggregate bandwidth consumption on all links, maximize the residual bandwidth on the most loaded link, and minimize the cumulative cost of a set of diverse paths.
sections.eli5: Constraints are the rules, like 'no toll roads' or 'must fit a big truck'. The objective is what counts as best, such as shortest or least crowded.

sections.title: Reliability, Scale and Recovery
sections.content:
The protocol SHOULD use an existing transport protocol that supports congestion control, defined for one transport only, and MUST NOT limit message size. It MUST support reliable transmission. The transport or the protocol must detect lost or corrupted messages, retransmit them, handle out-of-order and duplicate messages, provide flow control and back-pressure, and detect failure rapidly. It MUST support indication of congestion state and rate limitation state, because many PCCs may ask at once after a link failure.

On scale, the protocol MUST scale at least linearly. The order-of-magnitude figures include 1000 PCCs per domain, 100 PCEs per domain, 20 domains, an average of 10 path request messages per second per PCE, and bursts of 100 per second per PCE within a 10-second interval. Each side MUST be able to check that the other is alive and tell node failures from connectivity failures, and MUST resynchronize after a failure.

For rerouting, a request MUST be able to say it is for LSP restoration and include the previously computed path and the failed element. Reoptimization requests MUST also be able to include the old path, which helps the PCE avoid double bandwidth accounting.
sections.eli5: The planner must keep working when everyone asks at once after a road closes, notice when the phone line dies, and pick up where it left off.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The protocol MUST include provisions against spoofing (such as authentication), snooping (such as encryption) and denial of service. Key management MUST be provided for the authenticity and integrity of messages. A new element on the network brings risks: any host could impersonate a PCC and learn path details, or impersonate a PCE and spoof responses. Multi-domain use raises confidentiality concerns. Local policy SHOULD be able to forbid a PCE from returning explicit paths, in which case it MUST return an error. The protocol MUST also let operators limit the risk of a PCC using complex objectives to exhaust a PCE.

For manageability, the protocol MUST be modeled and controlled through MIB modules, with separate modules for PCCs and PCEs, statistics on malformed, unauthorized and congestion-discarded messages, notifications, and built-in diagnostic tools.
sections.eli5: Because the planner knows how the whole network is laid out, only trusted parties should be able to ask it, and nobody should be able to pose as it. Operators also need dashboards to watch it.
